What Is a Marketing Funnel, and When Does It Help?

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 18 May 2026 · 8-minute read · Growth

A marketing funnel is a model of the stages a stranger passes through before becoming a customer: awareness, consideration, evaluation, purchase and retention. It helps teams find where potential customers stop making progress. It is less useful as a map of how any individual buys, because research from Google and Gartner shows buyers loop back and skip stages. Use it to find the one stage that limits revenue now, and be wary of any plan described as "full-funnel".

The funnel is the oldest model in marketing: a wide opening of people who have never heard of you, narrowing through stages of awareness, interest and evaluation, to a small number who buy. Everyone uses it, and it is worth understanding both for what it explains and for what it hides.

Where the funnel comes from

The earliest version is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action. EBSCO's reference entry credits Elias St. Elmo Lewis, an American advertising adviser, with coining it around 1898, and Edward Strong with refining it in the 1920s. Later versions added stages after the sale, such as retention and satisfaction, because the model's original endpoint, a purchase, stopped being where most of the value sat.

The stages, plainly:

StageWhat is true of the personWeak measureBetter measure
AwarenessKnows the company or category existsImpressions, reachUnprompted recall, branded search volume
ConsiderationSees the problem as theirs; includes you as an optionPage viewsReturn visits, sign-ups, questions asked
EvaluationActively comparing options and looking for proofContent downloadsDemo requests, trials, pricing views, sales conversations
PurchaseBuysBookings aloneRevenue, and the cost of all stages above divided by buyers
Retention and advocacyStays, expands, tells othersSatisfaction scoresRetention, expansion, referrals

The right-hand column is where the funnel earns its keep. Every stage has a cheap measure that moves easily and a harder one closer to the decision.

What the model gets right

People do move through states of knowledge, and those states need different things. Someone who has never heard of a category will not respond to a comparison chart, and someone comparing three vendors does not need to be told the problem exists. Matching content and channel to stage is the funnel's lasting lesson. Our piece on content with a job turns that lesson into a commissioning brief.

The model also makes conversion between stages visible. If a thousand people reach evaluation and ten buy, the problem is in evaluation, not in awareness. Spending more at the top makes it worse, because it pushes more people into the stage that is already failing them.

What the model gets wrong

Real buying is not linear. Google's consumer insights team, in research published in July 2020 that simulated 310,000 purchase scenarios, described a "messy middle" between trigger and purchase, where shoppers "loop through these twin modes of exploration and evaluation" until they decide. Gartner's model of B2B buying says the same about business purchases: buyers complete six buying jobs, from problem identification to consensus creation, and loop back to revisit each at least once. Gartner also found buyers spend only 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers.

So people enter at any stage, skip stages and return to earlier ones. They are influenced by things no funnel records: a colleague's recommendation, a podcast heard six months ago, a competitor's failure. In B2B the "person" in the funnel is often a group; Gartner puts a typical buying group for a complex purchase at six to ten decision makers. The funnel describes an average path that almost nobody takes individually. Our explainer on the buying committee covers what that means for who you are actually moving.

The model also encourages the belief that more at the top produces more at the bottom. It does not, if the middle is broken or the top is filled with the wrong people. A funnel full of unqualified awareness is expensive at every stage below.

The funnel describes an average path that almost nobody takes individually. Use it to find the leak, not to script the buyer.

Why "full-funnel" usually means nothing

"Full-funnel marketing" is the claim that a company or agency addresses every stage. In practice it usually means spending in every channel without deciding which stage is the constraint. It sounds thorough. It is often the absence of a decision dressed as completeness.

There is a real argument for investing above the funnel. The B2B Institute at LinkedIn, drawing on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argues that about 95% of potential buyers are not in market at any given time, which is why brand-building reaches people long before they buy. That argument is about awareness as a long-term asset. It is not a licence to spread one quarter's budget evenly across five stages.

A useful plan identifies which stage is limiting revenue right now and concentrates there. Each constraint calls for different spending, and spending on the others is waste until the constraint moves:

SymptomLikely constraintWhere the next quarter's effort goes
Nobody has heard of you; branded search is flatAwarenessReach in channels your buyers use, earned media, partners
Traffic but few sign-ups or questionsConsiderationPositioning, the offer, landing pages (conversion rate optimization)
Trials or demos that do not convertEvaluation or productProof, onboarding, the product itself, sales process
Customers who leave in year oneRetentionFit at the point of sale, delivery, customer success

How to use it well

Draw the funnel with real numbers for the last quarter: how many at each stage, and the conversion between each. Find the stage where the drop is largest relative to what a healthy business in your category would show. Put the next quarter's effort there. Redraw it each quarter, because the constraint moves once it is fixed.

Illustrative example: the leak was not at the top
Decision
Hold paid acquisition flat for a quarter and move the budget to the evaluation stage.
Reason and owner
The quarter's funnel showed 4,000 site visitors, 400 sign-ups, 120 demos and 6 customers. Visitor-to-demo rates were in line with the firm's history; demo-to-customer had halved. The head of growth owned the change.
What changed
The team rebuilt the demo around the buyer's own data and added a security answers document. Demo-to-customer recovered over the next two quarters with no increase in spend.

Illustrative: a composite of a B2B software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

The numbers in the example are illustrative, but the method is general: a funnel is a diagnostic, and a diagnostic is only useful if it changes where the next pound or dollar goes. Our piece on demand generation economics sets out how to put a cost on each stage.

Finally, for a company the ad platforms restrict, the top of the funnel is partly closed in the crowded channels and open in the thinly bid ones. The funnel does not change. Where it can be filled does.

lowob takeaways

  • Diagnose, do not dictate. Funnel stages show where people stall; they do not describe any one buyer's path.
  • Measure close to the decision. Each stage has a cheap metric and a better one; use the better one.
  • Find the constraint. The largest abnormal drop between stages is where the next quarter goes.
  • Treat "full-funnel" as a question. Ask which stage is the constraint before approving spend across all of them.

Common questions

What are the stages of a marketing funnel?

The common stages are awareness, consideration (or interest), evaluation (or intent), purchase, and retention and advocacy. Each needs different content and is measured differently, from branded search at the top to retention and referral at the bottom.

Is the marketing funnel still relevant?

As a diagnostic, yes: conversion between stages shows where people stall. As a description of how people buy, it is weak. Google's messy-middle research and Gartner's B2B buying jobs both show buyers looping back rather than moving in order.

What does full-funnel marketing mean?

It is the claim that a plan or agency covers every stage. In practice it often means spending across all channels without deciding which stage is limiting revenue. A better plan names the constraint and concentrates there.

How do I find the bottleneck in my funnel?

Count the people at each stage for the last quarter, calculate conversion between stages, and compare each rate with your own history or a credible benchmark. The stage with the largest abnormal drop is the constraint.
